html:
In 1763 Frederick the Great issued the General School Regulations, which required all children in rural Prussia to attend school from about age five to thirteen or fourteen.

His father had ordered schooling in 1717, but it was poorly enforced. The new rules set out school hours, what was taught, teacher qualifications and fines for parents who kept children home. Many villages still lacked trained teachers, often old soldiers, but the principle that the state should make every child learn to read was set.

After Prussia's defeat by Napoleon in 1806, reformers led by Wilhelm von Humboldt rebuilt the system with teacher training, state exams and the gymnasium. Visitors came to study it. The American Horace Mann praised it in the 1840s, and it shaped public schools in the United States, the rest of Germany, Scandinavia and Meiji Japan. Prussia had some of the highest literacy rates in Europe by the 1800s.
sum: In 1763 Frederick the Great issued the General School Regulations, which required all children in rural Prussia to attend school from about age five to thirteen or fourteen.
